clinicalPearls: Cord prolapse is descent of the umbilical cord below the presenting part once the membranes have ruptured (overt prolapse); a cord lying beside the presenting part is occult prolapse, and a cord below the presenting part with intact membranes is a cord presentation
It is an acute obstetric emergency because cord compression, together with vasospasm from cooling and handling, interrupts fetal oxygenation and produces rapid fetal hypoxia and bradycardia

Risk factors reflect a poorly applied presenting part: malpresentation such as breech or transverse lie, prematurity, polyhydramnios, a high or unengaged presenting part, multiparity, multiple pregnancy, and a long cord
Iatrogenic cases follow artificial rupture of membranes with a high presenting part, amnioinfusion, external cephalic version, or other intrauterine manipulation
Diagnosis is by seeing or palpating the cord in the vagina or at the introitus, or by an abrupt fetal heart rate abnormality such as variable decelerations or bradycardia soon after membrane rupture

Immediate measures relieve cord compression: elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, position the woman knee-chest or head-down in the left lateral posture, minimise handling of the cord, and consider tocolysis
Definitive management is expedited delivery, most often by emergency caesarean section, unless vaginal birth is imminent and would be quicker
Outcome depends chiefly on the interval from diagnosis to delivery, so regular drills, early recognition, and rapid transfer are central to safe management
reference.pathophysiology: The umbilical cord supplies the fetus with oxygenated blood, and vessel patency depends on the cord not being compressed. A presenting part that does not fill the pelvic inlet, as in malpresentation, prematurity, an unengaged head, or polyhydramnios with sudden decompression at membrane rupture, leaves a space through which the cord can slip below or beside the fetus. Once the cord lies below the presenting part with ruptured membranes, descent of the fetus and uterine contractions compress the cord against the bony pelvis and occlude the umbilical vessels. In addition, exposure of the cord to the cooler vaginal environment and physical handling provoke reflex vasospasm. The combination of mechanical occlusion and vasospasm reduces or abolishes umbilical blood flow, causing fetal hypoxaemia, bradycardia, and, if unrelieved, hypoxic-ischaemic injury or death.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of acute fetal bradycardia such as placental abruption, uterine rupture, or maternal hypotension
Cord presentation with intact membranes rather than frank prolapse
Prolonged deceleration from rapid cervical dilatation or uterine hyperstimulation
Maternal supine hypotension reducing uteroplacental flow
Prolapse of another structure mistaken for cord at examination
additionalInvestigations: Immediate vaginal examination to confirm the cord below or alongside the presenting part and to assess cervical dilatation
Palpation of the cord for pulsation as a bedside marker of fetal viability
Continuous cardiotocography or fetal heart rate monitoring
Bedside ultrasound to confirm presentation and fetal viability if immediately available
Maternal observations of pulse and blood pressure to exclude contributory hypotension
Urgent preoperative bloods including full blood count and group-and-save or crossmatch
Umbilical cord arterial blood gas at delivery to document the degree of acidaemia
redFlags: Fetal bradycardia or deep variable decelerations following rupture of the membranes
Visible or palpable cord at or beyond the introitus
Cord prolapse occurring remote from theatre or skilled help
reference.prognosis: When recognised promptly and followed by rapid delivery, most babies do well. Delay in relieving cord compression is associated with hypoxic-ischaemic injury and perinatal death, and outcomes are worse when prolapse occurs outside hospital.
pitfalls: Performing artificial rupture of membranes with a high or ill-applied presenting part, precipitating prolapse
Attempting to replace or excessively handle the cord, which aggravates vasospasm
Failing to maintain continuous elevation of the presenting part until delivery
Delaying delivery to complete investigations or transfer without maintaining decompression measures
Overlooking a cord presentation on examination in a woman with risk factors before the membranes rupture
references: RCOG Green-top Guideline on umbilical cord prolapse
Oxford Handbook of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
management: Immediate relief of cord compression by manually elevating the presenting part or filling the bladder, and minimising handling of the cord to avoid vasospasm
Positioning the woman knee-chest or head-down in the left lateral position to reduce pressure on the cord
Tocolysis to abolish uterine contractions and improve foetal oxygenation while preparing for delivery
Continuous cardiotocographic foetal heart rate monitoring, with cord pulsation used as a bedside marker of viability
Urgent delivery, usually by category-one caesarean section, or assisted vaginal birth if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent
Activation of the obstetric emergency response with neonatal resuscitation team present at delivery and anaesthetic support
